Guided Inquiry

1 · The packet

Let’s meet our particle. It moves freely in two dimensions, and the surface you see is |ψ(x, y, t)|², the probability density for finding it at (x, y), normalised so that ∫∫|ψ|² dx dy = 1. Left alone, the packet spreads out. Soon you’ll measure its position and see what comes back.

2 · One measurement

Let’s start with the classical picture. There, the particle already sits at one definite point, and the hump only records our ignorance of which one. Let the packet spread, then measure its position. What do you think comes back?

3 · Core and surround

Now take a look at the colour map, which shows |ψ|² directly: a bright core fading into a dark surround where |ψ|² is small but never zero. If you measure many times over, how do you think the outcomes will divide between core and surround?

4 · Immediately after an outcome

Now for a twist. You measure a broad packet and it returns a point. Then, without letting any time pass, you measure the position again. Where do you think the second outcome will fall?

5 · After the collapse

One last experiment. This time the narrow packet left by the measurement is allowed to evolve freely, and its peak |ψ|² falls as time passes. If you measure the position much later, what do you expect? An outcome that is…

The Physics

Wavefunction collapse in 2D · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A free particle in two dimensions is described by a cloud of probability that spreads out on its own. This sim lets you watch the cloud spread and then measure the particle's position, which is where quantum probability meets a single result.

What you'll learn

  • How the height and colour of the display encode the probability density |ψ|².
  • How the width and peak of a free packet depend on time and on the starting width σ.
  • How a measurement outcome relates to the density.
  • What state the packet is in just after a measurement, and how it evolves from there.
One density, shown two ways: the heatmap colours it, the 3D surface raises it. Right: a cut through the surface along x. Schematic, not to scale.

What's on screen

  • Blue surface (3D view): its height at (x, y) is |ψ|² at that point.
  • Heatmap (the other view): the same |ψ|² as colour, with a colour bar on the right.
  • Green flash: the surface turns green for a moment when you press Measure.
  • Statistics: time, peak |ψ|², probability readouts, and the starting position.
  • Recent Collapses: the Final X and Final Y of your last 10 measurements.
See itStart a packet with width σ = 0.75 and let it run. Watch for: the blue surface flattening as Time Elapsed counts up.

03

What the surface shows

The surface height, and the colour of the heatmap, are one quantity: the probability density |ψ(x, y, t)|². It is probability per unit area, so a single value is not a probability. Probabilities come from adding up density over a region, and the volume under the whole surface is exactly 1 at every moment.

The density the sim evaluates at every point of its mesh.
  • Total Probability reads 1, the volume under the whole surface. Visible Probability is the part inside the display square. It falls only when the tails of a very wide packet reach the edge.
  • The sim evaluates only |ψ|². It never shows the phase of ψ.
  • The heatmap colour scale is fixed to the opening peak 1/(2πσ²). A packet that spreads fades toward dark blue instead of being rescaled.
See itSwitch to the heatmap at the opening packet. Watch for: a bright yellow core fading to dark blue, and the colour bar topping out at the Peak |ψ|² reading.
04

How a free packet spreads

Nothing pushes the packet, so it only widens. It stays a Gaussian, and its width after time t (in units with ħ = m = 1) is:

Width σ(t) and the peak that follows from it.
  • The volume under the surface stays 1, so a wider packet must be lower: the peak falls as 1/σ(t)².
  • The peak halves at τ = 2σ², when the width has grown by √2. The width doubles at t₂ = 2√3 σ².
  • A packet that starts narrower spreads sooner: τ is four times shorter when σ is halved.
A cut along x for σ = 0.75, at t = 0, 2σ² and 6σ².
σ speed

These sliders move the sim too. Changing σ restarts the run at t = 0.

See itRun the packet until t = 2σ² and pause. Watch for: Peak |ψ|² at about half of its opening value.
See itRun σ = 0.70, then σ = 1.40, each until its peak halves. Watch for: the narrower packet halving about four times sooner.
05

Where a measurement lands

A measurement returns one point (xm, ym), not a patch. Where it falls is random, but the odds are set by the density: the probability of landing in a region A is |ψ|² added up over A (the Born rule). The sim draws x and y from the exact Gaussian, restricted to the display square, so its odds are |ψ|² renormalised on that square.

The Born rule, and the one correction the sim makes for its finite window.
  • Bright regions are likely and dark regions are rare, but dark does not mean forbidden.
  • The most likely single point is the centre. The most likely distance from the centre is r = σ(t), because rings farther out have more area.
  • P(r < kσ(t)) = 1 − e−k²/2. That is 39% inside σ(t) and 86% inside 2σ(t). The familiar 68% is for one coordinate alone.
  • Each Measure replaces the packet (next section), so a second press in the same run does not sample this hump. Start a fresh packet for each outcome.
Illustration: twelve outcomes placed at the quantiles of the radial law, not real draws. Right: the law itself.
See itMeasure 150 fresh packets in a row, each at t = 0, and tally where they land. Watch for: about 39% inside r = σ and about 86% inside 2σ, with scatter of a few percent.
06

What a measurement leaves behind

After the outcome (xm, ym), the sim replaces the packet with a new Gaussian of width σ, the Measurement Width, centred on the outcome. The old density is gone.

One outcome is drawn, and the state it came from is replaced.
  • This models a measurement with finite resolution σ. A perfectly sharp position state cannot be normalised, and real detectors have finite resolution.
  • A repeat measurement straight away is not guaranteed to agree with the first. It lands within about σ of it.
  • One slider sets both widths. Measuring just after Play barely narrows the packet, because it has not spread yet. Measure after it has spread and the width drops back to σ.
  • The sim applies the textbook collapse rule. Interpretations of quantum mechanics differ on what this step is physically, and the sim takes no side.
One Measure at t = 1.95, drawn as a cut through the surface before and after. The outcome xm = 1.50 is an illustrative draw.
See itLet the packet spread until its width has doubled, then press Measure. Watch for: the surface jumping from a low, broad hump to a tall, narrow spike at a new spot.
07

Spreading starts again

The new packet is free, like the first one, and it spreads the same way from the moment of the measurement tm:

σ(t) = √( σ² + ( (t − tm) / 2σ )² )  for  t ≥ tm
The packet's own clock restarts at the measurement. Time Elapsed keeps counting.
  • The same σ sets the new packet's τ = 2σ², so its peak halves again after the same time as the first packet's did.
  • Nothing pulls the packet back toward the original centre. It is centred on the outcome, and it widens from there.
  • Measure again long after the first outcome and the new outcomes scatter over a patch of size about σ(t − tm). That patch grows with the waiting time.
See itMeasure, then let the new packet run for a time 2σ². Watch for: the new spike's peak falling to about half, just as the first packet's did.
08

Where it matters

Restoring units, the doubling time is t₂ = 2√3 mσ²/ħ. It grows as the mass m and as the square of the width.

  • Electrons. A free electron prepared with a width of 1 nm doubles it in about 30 fs. Tight localisation is short-lived unless something holds the electron in place.
  • Heavy objects. A 1 µg grain localised to 1 µm needs about a million years to double. On any human timescale it does not spread, which is why everyday objects look classical.
  • Matter-wave interferometry. Interferometers for atoms and molecules rely on each packet being wider than the spacing between the paths it must pass through.
Go deeper: why a sharper packet spreads sooner
  • A Gaussian packet that starts with width σ has momentum spread Δpx = ħ/2σ in each direction. Squeezing the position raises the momentum spread, and the momentum spread is what widens the packet.
  • At t = 0 the product ΔxΔpx = ħ/2, the smallest the uncertainty relation allows.
09

Summary

In one line. The surface is the density |ψ|². A measurement draws one point from it, replaces the packet with a narrow one centred on that point, and the new packet spreads again.

Key points

  • The packet's width grows as σ(t) = √(σ² + (t/2σ)²), so its peak falls while the volume stays 1.
  • One outcome per measurement, drawn from |ψ|²: 39% inside r = σ(t), 86% inside 2σ(t).
  • After a measurement the packet has width σ, sits on the outcome, and spreads again from t − tm = 0.

Common mix-ups

  • "A measurement just reads off where the particle already was." In the rule the sim uses, the outcome is drawn from |ψ|² and the packet is then replaced. Whether the particle had a position beforehand is an interpretation question the sim does not settle.
  • "The dark surround is forbidden." |ψ|² is small there but not zero. Rare is not impossible.
  • "A measurement pins the particle down for good." The new packet starts spreading at once, exactly as the first one did.

Things to try on your own

  • Pick a width σ, work out τ = 2σ², press Play, and check Time Elapsed when Peak |ψ|² reaches half its opening value.
  • Let the packet spread past t₂, press Measure, and compare Peak |ψ|² before and after.
  • Repeat Reset, Play, Measure twenty times. Count how many Final X, Final Y pairs have √(X² + Y²) below σ = 0.75 and compare with 39%.
